result: The authors used a semi-supervised deep learning workflow (DeepForest) based on RGB imagery to detect individual tree crowns, with LiDAR data used only for post-hoc filtering of objects <3m tall. The workflow involved pre-training on ImageNet and weak labels from LiDAR algorithms, then training on 10,000 hand-annotated crowns. The authors tested but found no improvement from directly incorporating LiDAR data into the CNN for crown detection.
evaluation: Reviewers expressed strong surprise that LiDAR data was not used for crown segmentation itself, stating 'The reviewers are very surprised that you do not use the LiDAR data in the segmentation of the single tree crowns.' They questioned why height was not used as a fourth dimension and suggested that LiDAR-based ITC methods could remedy error sources like shaded crowns and sub-dominant trees. The authors' explanation that data fusion did not improve performance (C41-C42) was provided but reviewers clearly expected more integration of LiDAR for the core detection task.

result: The DeepForest workflow achieved 79.1% recall and 72.6% precision on image-annotated data. Adding the LiDAR 3m height threshold increased precision by 7.0% but decreased recall by 0.2%. The model generalizes well across geographic sites and forest conditions.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the reported accuracy metrics (~70% detection rate mentioned in summary) without direct challenge. The acceptance summary states the 'accuracy of the automatic detection was about 70%' and reviewers did not question these performance figures, though they suggested comparisons with LiDAR-based methods.

result: Field stem recall rate was 69.4%, similar to bounding box recall from image-annotated data. This analysis is conservative due to challenges in aligning field-collected spatial data with remote sensing data, and some good predictions were counted as false positives due to positional errors.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge the field validation results. The acceptance summary acknowledges the comparison with 'field-measured stem positions and height and crown data' without expressing concerns about the methodology or results.

result: Predicted heights showed good correspondence with field measurements, with RMSE of 1.73m using a linear mixed model. Performance varied by forest type (stronger in open canopies, weaker in dense canopies). There was a systematic bias toward taller predictions, partially explained by temporal gaps between field and remote sensing data collection.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the height validation results without challenge. The acceptance summary notes 'the height of the trees with an accuracy of roughly 2 m RMSE' without expressing concerns. The authors' interpretation that this represents 'reasonably accurate' measures was not disputed.

result: The model exhibits systematic biases including undersegmentation (grouping multiple trees as single crowns) and conservative crown extent estimation. The authors acknowledge ambiguity in defining individual trees, noting that what appears as one crown may be multiple trees or vice versa, and that distinguishing individuals can be subjective even in field surveys.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these acknowledged limitations. The discussion of model biases and the inherent ambiguity in crown delineation appears to have been accepted as a transparent acknowledgment of methodological constraints.

result: NEON's LiDAR has lower point density (~6 pts/m², highly variable, often <4 pts/m²) compared to typical studies (15-100+ pts/m²). This sparse density, combined with geographic variation and lack of joint RGB-LiDAR pretraining data, explains why direct LiDAR incorporation into the CNN did not improve performance.
evaluation: While reviewers did not directly dispute the LiDAR density claims, the second round decision letter requests the authors 'make it clearer why LiDAR currently could not further improve the detection of individual crowns (because of low resolution and inconsistencies across multiple sites in available LiDAR data).' This indicates reviewers found the explanation insufficient and wanted stronger justification for not using LiDAR-based methods.

result: The dataset reveals continental-scale patterns including relationships between forest density and tree allometry (denser forests have narrower crowns for given height), with variation by vegetation type. Comparisons between field plots and full-site remote sensing show deviations in tree density estimates, highlighting that even well-stratified field sampling can differ from continuous remote sensing.
evaluation: The second round decision letter states reviewers want 'more concrete suggestions what could be done with the data' and notes 'even though you show a figure with densities, in the corresponding paragraph it is not really discussed why density is so extremely important in forest ecology.' Reviewers cite Barrufol et al. and note that density and biodiversity are 'probably the most important variable you eventually would like to assess.' This indicates the ecological applications were underdeveloped.

result: The dataset is limited to sun-exposed canopy trees and is not appropriate for analyses requiring subcanopy characterization. However, many major ecological questions are driven by large individuals, and biomass estimation is largely driven by canopy rather than understory trees.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this limitation in the acceptance summary, stating the data provides 'a large step forward from pixel-level data' despite being limited to canopy trees. The acceptance summary explicitly notes the dataset is for 'individual trees' from 'airborne remote sensing,' implicitly accepting the canopy-only limitation.

result: Individual-level tree data bridges the gap between local field surveys and broad-scale satellite data. It connects remote sensing pixels to fundamental ecological units, enables comparison with field measurements, and serves as a foundation for species classification, trait mapping, and mortality analyses. Technical barriers have prevented most researchers from accessing such data despite its importance.
evaluation: The acceptance summary strongly endorses this motivation, stating the data 'offer a large step forward from pixel-level data for ecologists interested in forest structure, size-density-diversity relationships and how these affect ecosystem functioning, arguably the most important topic in current forest research.' However, reviewers wanted more concrete discussion of applications (see second round comments).

result: The NEON Crowns dataset contains 104,675,304 tree crowns from 37 NEON sites with co-registered RGB and LiDAR data from 2018-2019. Trees are defined as plants >3m tall. Each crown includes spatial position, bounding box area, height estimate, year, site, and confidence score (≥0.15). Data are provided as shapefiles and CSV files, openly licensed and archived on Zenodo.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the dataset description without challenge. The acceptance summary confirms 'a large data set of tree positions, heights and crown areas from 37 NEON sites across North America' and notes the data are from 'over 100 million individual canopy trees.'

result: A web visualization tool was developed using ViSUS WebViewer allowing users to view trees at full site scale with zoom/pan capabilities down to 20m scale. NEON sites typically have 100-400 tiles in their airborne footprint.
evaluation: Reviewers did not comment on the visualization tool, suggesting implicit acceptance of this supporting resource for the dataset.

result: The LiDAR-derived 3m threshold is important for distinguishing trees from shrubs in sparsely vegetated landscapes. Evaluation metrics are defined with true positives requiring >50% intersection-over-union, with recall as proportion of annotated crowns matched and precision as proportion of predictions matching annotations.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these methodological definitions. The metrics and threshold rationale were accepted as part of the validation framework.

result: The authors discuss various potential applications including tree growth and mortality tracking, foliar biochemistry, carbon storage, species classification, trait mapping, fire resistance, pest management, and understanding landscape-scale patterns. Individual-level data enables direct connection to field measurements and tracking of ecological processes. The dataset can support machine learning applications and broad-scale forest monitoring.
evaluation: The second round decision letter explicitly requests 'more concrete suggestions what could be done with the data,' stating 'You do mention the value of individual data as opposed to pixel data in very general terms' but want specific discussion of why density is important in forest ecology and how biodiversity could be assessed. Reviewers cite specific papers (Barrufol et al., Liang et al., Huang et al.) as examples of the concrete applications they expect to see discussed.

result: The authors speculate about future improvements including establishing understory-canopy relationships, updating with higher-density LiDAR and improved algorithms to add subcanopy trees, combining terrestrial and airborne LiDAR, and potentially using hyperspectral data to separate neighboring trees.
evaluation: The second round decision letter requests clarity on 'what would be needed and hopefully will become available to include LiDAR more fully for future improvements of the data set (higher resolution data consistently available across all sites plus methods development).' This suggests reviewers wanted these future directions articulated but accepted them as reasonable goals.

result: The authors acknowledge the need to propagate uncertainty in downstream analyses, emphasize ongoing validation needs through field surveys and community annotation, and position this as the first version in an iterative improvement process. They assert current accuracy is sufficient for many cross-scale forest structure questions.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this framing. The acceptance of the manuscript despite acknowledged limitations suggests reviewers agreed the current version has value while recognizing room for improvement.

result: The model has a single 'Tree' class which prevents differentiation between non-trees and objects lacking training data. It was trained to ignore buildings but produces errors on novel objects (weather stations, buoys, oil wells). NEON data sometimes has imaging artifacts from co-registration issues causing poor segmentation. Designing models to identify unknown objects is an active research area.
evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these acknowledged limitations and error sources. The transparent discussion of model failures appears to have been accepted as appropriate acknowledgment of current constraints.
